alternatives.at: Direct real estate: NOI, cap rates
alternatives.say: Alright, here's the idea with direct real estate. Real assets like buildings, gold and collectibles often have low or even negative correlation with stocks and bonds. Investment property draws people for two reasons: leverage, meaning mostly borrowed money, and tax deductions for mortgage interest, property taxes and depreciation. Now the value ladder. Potential gross income is all the rents plus other income like laundry and parking. Subtract vacancy and collection losses for effective gross income. Subtract cash operating expenses and you land on net operating income. Value equals NOI divided by the cap rate, which you estimate from comparable recent sales. Walk Maple Court: twenty units at twelve hundred a month, plus six thousand of other income, gives PGI of two hundred ninety-four thousand. Six percent vacancy leaves about two hundred seventy-six thousand. Take out ninety-eight thousand of operating expenses and NOI is about one hundred seventy-eight thousand. Divide by seven percent and it's worth about two point five five million, the most a prudent buyer should pay. A higher cap rate means a lower value. Leverage cuts both ways: twenty-five thousand down on a two hundred fifty thousand building that rises ten percent doubles your money, and a ten percent drop wipes out your equity. Raw land earns nothing and costs money every year, so it needs a big expected gain. The exam trap: NOI is the property's cash flow, not the investor's, so any answer that subtracts mortgage interest or depreciation is wrong. To a client: before you fall in love with the building, let's see what it actually earns after vacancies and running costs, and that tells us the ceiling on what to pay.

Alright, indirect real estate. RELPs and REITs let people own real estate without the high cost and illiquidity of buying buildings. A real estate limited partnership is run by a general partner, the syndicator, who keeps an interest, charges fees and is liable for all partnership acts. Limited partners' liability is capped at what they invested, they have no management role, the interest is generally illiquid, and the passive activity rules apply. A REIT is a corporation run by a board of directors. Many trade on exchanges. REIT income is portfolio income, and losses are capital losses, not passive ones. The REIT pays no entity-level federal tax if it distributes at least ninety percent of net annual earnings and at least seventy-five percent of gross income comes from real estate. Equity REITs own property and hedge inflation well, while mortgage REITs make loans and tend to suffer when inflation rises. Then a CMO splits mortgage cash flows into sequential tranches. Principal goes to Tranche A until it's paid off, then B, then C, while Z gets nothing until the others retire. So a short-horizon client wanting the least rate risk takes A. Z, with the longest wait, carries the most interest rate risk and behaves like a zero, taxed on interest it hasn't paid in cash. The exam trap: REIT shareholders are not subject to the passive activity rules, that's the RELP investor's problem, and a REIT has a board, not a general partner. To a client: a REIT lets you own a slice of many buildings and sell tomorrow, while a partnership can lock your money up for years.

Alright, here's the idea behind options. The buyer gets a right, not an obligation. A call is the right to buy at the strike price, a put is the right to sell, on or before expiration. The writer collects the premium and takes on the obligation, and one contract covers one hundred shares. Now the payoff grid. Buy a call: bullish, unlimited gain, loss capped at the premium, breakeven at strike plus premium. Write a naked call: bearish or neutral, gain is the premium, loss is unlimited. Buy a put: bearish, max gain is strike minus premium, max loss is the premium, breakeven is strike minus premium. Write a put: bullish or neutral, gain is the premium, loss is strike minus premium. The buyer's gain is the writer's loss. Intrinsic value for a call is stock minus strike, for a put it's strike minus stock, never below zero, and time value is the rest of the premium. Kestrel trades at fifty-two. The fifty-dollar call at four ten has two dollars intrinsic and two ten of time value, breaking even at fifty-four ten. The fifty-five put at four sixty has three dollars intrinsic, one sixty of time value, and breaks even at fifty forty. Its writer makes at most four hundred sixty a contract. In the money ignores the premium, profitable does not. The exam trap: a long put's gain is not unlimited, it's capped at strike minus premium because a stock can't fall below zero. Only the long call's gain and the naked call's loss are unlimited. To a client: buying an option is like paying for a reservation, you can walk away and lose only the deposit.

alternatives.at: Option pricing models and option taxation
alternatives.say: Alright, good news first: you won't calculate an option price on the exam. You need the models' assumptions, which way each input pushes a call's value, and how premiums hit basis or gain. The binomial model moves the stock up or down in steps, and more steps bring it closer to Black-Scholes. Black-Scholes values a European call assuming prices change continuously, captured by volatility. When the stock price, time to expiration, volatility or the risk-free rate rises, the call is worth more. When the exercise price rises, the call is worth less. Put-call parity says call minus put equals stock price minus the present value of the strike, and if it breaks, riskless arbitrage is possible. Now taxes. If a call is exercised, the holder adds the premium to the stock's basis, and the writer adds it to the amount realized. If a put is exercised, the holder subtracts the premium from the amount realized, and the writer subtracts it from the basis of the stock bought. If the option expires, the holder has a capital loss and the writer a short-term capital gain. Walk it: Lia writes a forty-five put for two dollars and gets assigned, so her basis is forty-three hundred. Her neighbor exercises a forty-five call bought for two, so his basis is forty-seven hundred. Had Lia's put expired, she'd report a two hundred dollar short-term gain. The exam trap: a higher strike lowers a call's value, because the stock must climb further to have intrinsic value. To a client: if your call is worth more than its exercise value, sell it rather than exercising early, because exercising throws away the time value.

Alright, how people actually use options: buy them to speculate, write covered calls for income, and buy protective puts to hedge. Speculation gives more leverage than margin, which needs at least fifty percent cash. Your loss stops at the premium, but options expire, so the move has to come in time. A covered call means you own the shares and write calls. You keep the premium but give up gains above the strike, and it works best in a sideways market. A protective put means you own the shares and buy puts, which floors you at the strike, but it's costly and temporary. Walk Nadia. She owns two hundred shares bought at thirty and writes two calls with a thirty-three strike for a dollar twenty each. If the stock ends at thirty-six, her shares get called at thirty-three and she makes eight hundred forty, and the move above thirty-three belongs to the buyer. At thirty-one, the calls expire and she keeps the premium and the shares. At twenty-five, she loses seven hundred sixty, because the premium only cushions a dollar twenty a share. Compare a protective put: own at fifty, buy a forty-seven put for a dollar fifty, and the most you can lose is four fifty a share. The exam trap: a short seller hedges with a call, not a put, because the risk is a rising price. To a client: selling calls on stock you own pays you rent while you wait, but if it takes off you sell at the agreed price, so only do it on shares you'd be happy to part with.

Alright, the riskier and fancier strategies. A naked call means writing a call without owning the shares. It's the riskiest of all, with a theoretically unlimited loss, which is why brokers require high account minimums. A naked put is moderately conservative: the most you can lose is strike minus premium, and people often write them on stocks they'd like to own. A covered put is shorting the stock and writing a put, the mirror of a covered call. A long straddle buys a call and a put at the same strike and expiration, because you expect a big move but don't know which way. A short straddle writes both, betting on little movement. And a zero-cost collar means owning the stock, buying a put and writing a call, so the call premium pays for the put. Walk the straddle: at a forty strike, the call costs two twenty and the put one eighty, four dollars total, so you only profit below thirty-six or above forty-four. Now Yusuf's collar: his stock, bought at forty, is now ninety. He buys an eighty-five put for three and writes a hundred-dollar call for three, so the net cost is zero, and his value is locked between eighty-five and one hundred until expiration. A naked put written at thirty for a dollar seventy-five costs twenty-eight twenty-five a share if assigned. The exam trap: a straddle is not a hedge against small moves, because a long straddle loses both premiums if the price barely changes. To a client: a collar puts a floor under a big gain and pays for it by agreeing to sell above a ceiling, protection without writing a check.

Alright, futures. A futures contract obligates both sides to make or take delivery of a set amount of a commodity or financial asset at a future date and price. Long means you agree to buy and gain if the price rises, short means you agree to sell and gain if it falls. Unlike an option buyer, a futures trader can lose far more than the deposit. That deposit is the initial margin, roughly five to ten percent of contract value. Gains and losses are marked to market daily, and if equity drops below maintenance margin, you must restore it to the initial margin, immediately. Walk it: a speculator goes long one thousand-barrel contract at seventy dollars, with six thousand initial and forty-five hundred maintenance. The price settles at sixty-eight twenty, an eighteen hundred dollar loss, so equity is forty-two hundred, below maintenance, and that's a margin call. He deposits eighteen hundred to get back to the initial margin, not just three hundred. On hedging, the hedge is always opposite your cash position. A farmer who owns the crop does a short hedge and sells futures; a baker who needs wheat later does a long hedge and buys futures. Taxes: year-end net gains are split sixty percent long-term and forty percent short-term, so a nine thousand dollar gain is fifty-four hundred long and thirty-six hundred short. The exam trap: futures gains are capital gains even when the underlying would be inventory, and the sixty-forty split applies no matter how long you held. To a client: futures are a deposit on a deal that settles every day, and small moves can demand more money overnight.

Alright, tangible assets: collectibles like cards, coins, stamps and art, plus precious metals. Collectibles give you enjoyment and possible appreciation, but they trade in inefficient, illiquid markets. Precious metals get their value from forces outside financial markets, like fear of inflation, so they often move opposite to stocks, a hedge for a bearish stock market. Collectibles face a maximum long-term rate of twenty-eight percent, higher than for securities. They do act like a tax shelter: no tax until sale, usually no current income, and a step-up in basis at death. Walk Paolo's thirty thousand dollar long-term gain. From stock at his fifteen percent rate, the tax is forty-five hundred. From a coin collection taxed at the twenty-eight percent cap, it's eighty-four hundred. But if he holds the coins until death, his heirs get a stepped-up basis and the gain escapes capital gains tax. Gold's enemy is high real interest rates, because gold pays no income, so the opportunity cost is high. Gold miners are about twice as volatile as large caps, so prefer funds or large established firms, and an advisor may cap gold at about five to ten percent of a diversified portfolio. Natural resources come through partnerships, stocks or sector funds, with depletion and drilling deductions passing through, and high risk. The exam trap: a retiree heavy in tangibles faces liquidity risk, forced to sell into a weak, illiquid market to raise income. To a client: collect what you know and love, but keep enough liquid that you never have to sell the collection in a down market to pay bills.

Alright, foreign securities. Going overseas adds diversification and return potential, but brings two extra risks: exchange rate risk and country risk, meaning political events plus structural risks like confiscatory treatment of profits. Foreign markets are often more volatile, yet their low correlation with U.S. stocks, bonds and each other lowers overall portfolio risk. Accounting standards differ, so ratios may not compare. Emerging markets have low capitalization, questionable liquidity, currency and ownership restrictions, and weak regulation, but fast growth. Developed markets are large, liquid and stable, with U.S.-like transparency. Frontier markets are the smaller emerging economies, with even more risk. Know the fund labels: a global fund holds U.S. and foreign stocks, so it can overlap what you already own, while an international fund is non-U.S. only. Single-country funds are highly volatile with major currency risk. An ADR is a U.S. bank trust receipt for foreign shares that trades here in dollars. Walk Deshawn: he owns three U.S. stock funds and wants foreign exposure without researching foreign companies. A global fund would repeat U.S. names he already owns. Buying directly abroad means foreign currency, possibly illiquid exchanges and weaker reporting, too complex. The best fit is a diversified developed international fund plus a diversified emerging markets fund. The exam trap: ADRs trade and pay in dollars, but the dividends are converted from local currency, so currency risk is not eliminated. To a client: owning companies overseas means you also own their currency, which helps some years and hurts others, but because those markets don't move in lockstep with ours, they tend to steady the whole portfolio.

Alright, picture your money traveling. Before you buy a foreign security, a strong dollar helps, because it buys more foreign currency. While you hold it, you want the dollar to fall against that currency, so the proceeds convert back into more dollars. The rule works for anyone: an investor holding another country's securities wants their home currency to weaken during the holding period. The mechanics: restate every quote as how much foreign currency one dollar buys. Dollar cost is the foreign price divided by foreign units per dollar at purchase, dollar proceeds are the foreign sale value divided by foreign units per dollar at sale, and the return is proceeds minus cost, over cost. Walk the U.K. shares: buy for eight thousand pounds when a dollar buys point eight zero pounds, so the cost is ten thousand dollars. Sell for eighty-four hundred pounds when a dollar buys only point seven five, and the proceeds are eleven thousand two hundred dollars. That's twelve percent in dollars versus five percent in pounds, because the dollar weakened. If instead a dollar buys point eight four pounds at sale, the proceeds are just ten thousand, a zero return. A revalued, stronger dollar buys more foreign units and hurts a U.S. owner of foreign stock; a devalued, weaker dollar helps. The exam trap: a quote of a dollar twenty-five per pound means one dollar buys point eight zero pounds, so flip it with one over x before converting. To a client: your European fund's stocks rose, but you made less because the dollar strengthened, and when the dollar weakens the same holdings give you a boost, so currency risk cuts both ways.
